theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A senior policy officer at a ministry is asked to draft a briefing note for the Minister before a meeting with sugar cane farmers. What should she establish first?
options: How many pages the last briefing note on sugar ran to
Which fonts and colours the Minister likes best
Which colleagues have written for the Minister before
What the Minister needs to know and decide, and by when

questions.stem: Why do many ministerial briefing notes begin with a short summary of the issue and the action sought?
options: The background is never important to a Minister
Busy readers can grasp the point and decide quickly
The rules forbid any summary at the end of a note
It lets the writer leave out facts that do not fit

questions.stem: A draft Cabinet submission contains proposed tax changes that have not been announced. How should it be handled?
options: Marked confidential and shared only with those who need it
Emailed to all staff in the division so that they can comment
Printed and left in the shared tray for the director to collect
Saved on the shared drive with no limits on who can open it

questions.stem: What does the "need to know" principle mean for sensitive documents?
options: Anyone in the ministry may read a document if they ask
Only the Minister may ever read a sensitive document
Only people who need the information for their work see it
Documents are shared once the media already knows of them

questions.stem: Which section of a Cabinet submission sets out what the proposal will cost and how it will be paid for?
options: The background
The financial implications
The title page
The list of annexes

questions.stem: A ministry is preparing a Cabinet submission on a new fee for permits. Which step should come before it is finalised?
options: Sharing the draft with a journalist to test public reaction
Sending it to Cabinet first and consulting agencies later
Keeping it from the finance and legal units to save time
Consulting finance, legal officers and the agencies affected

questions.stem: A draft speech for the Minister says that 12,000 farmers have received grants. The officer is not sure of the figure. What should he do?
options: Check it against the programme's records before sending
Round it up to 15,000, since it will sound more impressive
Leave it in, as nobody checks speeches closely
Take every figure out of the speech to avoid the problem

questions.stem: A public officer is asked to draft a speech for a Minister to give at a party political rally. What should she do?
options: Write it, including attacks on the opposition party
Write it in her own time so no one at work knows
Explain that party political material is outside her role
Ask a colleague to write it and then put her name to it

questions.stem: A Member of Parliament has tabled a question for the Minister about delays at the ministry's licensing office. What is the officer's main task?
options: Prepare a reply that avoids giving any figures at all
Find out which officer told the MP about the problem
Draft a reply that blames the previous administration
Prepare an accurate, concise draft reply with notes

questions.stem: Along with a draft answer to a question in Parliament, why do officers often prepare notes on likely follow-up questions?
options: So that the Minister can avoid the main question
So the Minister is ready for any further questions
So that the notes can be handed to the Opposition
So that the draft answer itself can be kept vague

questions.stem: Which sentence is best for a letter that the Permanent Secretary will sign to a member of the public?
options: Pursuant to the aforementioned matter, your application is deemed refused.
We looked at your stuff and your thing has not gone through, sorry.
We have considered your application and regret that we cannot approve it.
Your application was refused for reasons that cannot be given.

questions.stem: A ministry must write to the family of an officer who died in an accident at work. Which approach to the letter is best?
options: Sincere, respectful and clear about support and next steps
Brief and formal, with no mention of the accident at all
Detailed on legal liability, to protect the ministry
Cheerful and upbeat, to lift the family's spirits

questions.stem: Before a press conference on a delayed hospital project, officers prepare a "lines to take" document. What is it?
options: A list of journalists who should not be allowed in
Agreed short answers to likely questions, for the speakers
A timetable showing the order in which people will speak
The full contract for the hospital project, for reporters

questions.stem: Why should officers write internal memos and reports as if they might one day be seen by the public?
options: Every internal memo must be published on the ministry website
Memos are always read aloud in Parliament after one year
The media are sent copies of all the memos every week
Under the access to information law, many may be requested

questions.stem: Several officers are editing a sensitive draft policy paper. What is the best way to avoid confusion?
options: Version control: numbered drafts, dates and a change log
Each officer saves a copy, and the copies are merged at the end
Each officer emails the draft to the whole division after editing
Everyone edits the same printout and crosses out the old text

questions.stem: An officer realises she has emailed a confidential draft Cabinet note to the wrong outside address. What should she do first?
options: Say nothing and hope the person does not open it
Delete her copy so there is no record of the mistake
Report it to her manager at once, as policy requires
Email the person and ask them to forward it back to her

questions.stem: Which practice keeps sensitive printed documents secure in an open-plan office?
options: Leaving them face down on the desk at lunch time
A clear-desk rule and locked storage when not in use
Keeping them in a desk tray marked "Confidential"
Printing on the shared printer and collecting them later

questions.stem: Which order of headings suits a ministerial briefing note?
options: Annexes, background, issue, recommendation, purpose
Background, history, more background, then a summary
Recommendation only, with no facts or options given
Purpose, issue, background, options, recommendation

questions.stem: A briefing note asks the Minister to choose how to deal with a backlog of land titles. What should the options section contain?
options: Only the option the writer prefers, described in detail
Every option ever suggested, with no comment on any
A few realistic options, each with pros, cons and costs
Options with their costs left out to keep the note short

questions.stem: What makes the recommendation in a briefing note sound?
options: It follows from the analysis and says what is to be decided
It uses strong words to push the reader to agree at once
It is left open so that the Minister can supply the reasons
It repeats the background word for word for emphasis

questions.stem: A Cabinet submission is due in three days, but the legal unit has not yet commented. What should the officer do?
options: Submit it without legal comments and hope it is approved
Follow up with the legal unit and warn her manager of the risk
Write the legal comments herself, since the deadline is close
Miss the deadline without telling anyone about the delay

questions.stem: Who should normally clear a sensitive letter before it goes to the Minister for signature?
options: Only the officer who drafted it, as she knows it best
The ministry's receptionist, who will dispatch the letter
The person to whom the letter is addressed, in advance
The officer's manager and the senior officers in the chain

questions.stem: Which feature most helps a speech written for a Minister to be delivered well?
options: Long sentences full of technical terms and statistics
As many figures as possible, each read out in full
Short sentences and a clear structure, written for the ear
Exactly the same text as the ministry's annual report

questions.stem: An officer is writing the report of a disciplinary investigation into a senior officer. Which approach is best?
options: Stick to facts and evidence, and keep opinion out
Include the rumours, so that the report is complete
Describe the senior officer's private life in detail
Write it so that it hints at the expected outcome

questions.stem: A draft report to the Permanent Secretary includes the names, addresses and medical details of 40 clients. What should the writer do?
options: Keep the details, since the report is only for senior staff
Add their phone numbers too, so the PS can call each one
Send the report by personal email so that it arrives faster
Remove or anonymise any details not needed for the purpose

questions.stem: Before a high-level report goes to a public body's board, what is the best final check?
options: Rely on the spell-checker alone to find any errors
Ask a colleague to check the facts, figures and wording
Read only the summary, since that is all the board reads
Check the font size and leave the content as it is

questions.stem: A Cabinet submission says a programme will cost J$180,000,000 and help 12,000 people. What is the cost per person?
A briefing note says a backlog of 4,800 files will be cleared by a team that closes 320 files a week. How many weeks will this take?
options: 12 weeks
16 weeks
15 weeks
20 weeks

questions.stem: What should the executive summary of a sensitive report to the Cabinet Secretary contain?
options: A copy of the full table of contents and the annexes
The main findings, their effects and the recommendations
Only the history of how the report came to be written
A personal note from the writer about the work involved

questions.stem: Why should a briefing note on a new water tariff point out the likely public and media reaction?
options: So the Minister can put off the decision for several years
So that the communications unit is not needed at the launch
So the note can blame the media for any later problems
So the Minister can weigh it and plan how to explain it

questions.stem: A director asks an officer to leave a finding out of a draft report because it will embarrass the Minister. What should the officer do?
options: Explain that impartial advice includes such findings
Delete the finding quietly, since the director asked her to
Leak the finding to the media to make sure it becomes known
Reword the finding so that it says the opposite thing

questions.stem: Which details must a formal ministry letter on a sensitive matter always include?
options: A friendly emoji to show goodwill to the reader
The writer's personal mobile number and home address
A file reference, the date and the signatory's title
Copies of every earlier letter on any other subject

questions.stem: The Minister wants an urgent one-page update on flood damage before a phone call in one hour. Which format is best?
options: A 40-page report with photographs and full annexes
A formal Cabinet submission with all its sections
A long email thread forwarded with no summary
A short briefing note with key facts and actions

questions.stem: A policy officer must explain a complex engineering report in a note for the Minister. What should she do?
options: Copy the engineers' text into the note without changes
Ask the engineers to check her plain-language summary
Leave out the engineering points the Minister may dislike
Put her own technical opinion in place of the engineers'

questions.stem: Which way of sending a confidential draft to a colleague in another ministry is best?
options: By a free personal email account, which is faster
By a messaging app on the officer's own phone
By the approved secure system, marked confidential
Printed and handed to a courier with no envelope

questions.stem: A Minister's office asks an officer to change the figures in a report so that a programme looks more successful. What should she do?
options: Decline, and raise it through proper channels
Change them, since the Minister's office has asked her to
Change them, but keep the true figures in her own files
Resign at once without giving anyone her reasons

questions.stem: A high-level report uses many abbreviations. What should the writer do?
options: Leave them, since senior readers will guess their meaning
Use as many as possible to keep the report short
Explain them only in a footnote on the last page
Spell each out when it first appears, or add a list

questions.stem: A Cabinet submission compares the costs of three options over five years. How are the figures best shown?
options: In a long paragraph, with every figure written in words
In a clear table with totals, checked twice
In a photograph of the officer's handwritten notes
In several separate annexes, with no summary table

questions.stem: A director returns an officer's draft speech with many changes. What is the best response?
options: Study the changes and ask about unclear points
Reject the changes, since the officer wrote the first draft
Send the original draft to the Minister without the changes
Complain to colleagues that the director changes everything

questions.stem: A press release on a new policy is marked "embargoed until 10:00 a.m. Thursday". What does this mean?
options: It must never be shared with the media
It may be published at once if a reporter asks
It must not be published before that time
Reporters may change it before they publish it

questions.stem: After a sensitive submission is approved, what should happen to the final version and the key drafts?
options: They should be deleted to stop any leaks in future
They should be filed in the official records system
They should be kept on the officer's own memory stick
They should be emailed to the officer's home address

questions.stem: A report on crime in a community is being written for the Minister. How should the community be described?
options: Using the labels that the media often use for the area
As a place with no hope, to show how bad things are
Without data, so that no one can question the report
Fairly and factually, avoiding stereotypes and blame

questions.stem: Which is NOT a usual part of preparing a Cabinet submission?
options: Consulting the ministries and agencies affected
Setting out the financial and legal implications
Sharing the draft with the media for comment
Stating clearly what Cabinet is asked to decide

questions.stem: An officer has two tasks due today: an urgent brief for the Minister's 3:00 p.m. meeting and a routine monthly report. What should she do?
options: Do the brief first; agree a new time for the report
Do the monthly report first, since it is a regular task
Do half of each and send both unfinished at 5:00 p.m.
Do neither and wait for the director to decide later

questions.stem: Which question is most useful when reviewing a high-level document before it goes up the chain?
options: Is it longer than the last document on this topic?
Does it use the newest terms in the field?
Will its style impress the readers who get it?
Is it accurate, clear and fit for its purpose?

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Give the four-letter abbreviation for the writing approach "bottom line up front", which puts the main point first.
What name is given to the document a ministry sends to Cabinet asking it to make a decision?
What term is used for a short document that gives a Minister the key facts on an issue before a meeting or decision?
What term is used for an extra question that a Member of Parliament may ask after the Minister has answered the main question?
What is the name for a section at the end of a submission that holds detailed supporting material, such as tables or legal texts?
What two-word term describes writing that the intended reader can understand the first time they read it?
What word describes blacking out or removing the sensitive parts of a document before it is released?
What word describes obtaining each required senior officer's approval of a document before it goes forward?
What is the name of the official written record of debates in Parliament?
What is the name of the official government publication in which new laws, regulations and official notices are published?
What is the title of the officer who heads Jamaica's public service and also serves as secretary to the Cabinet?
A Minister's speech should last 12 minutes, and she speaks at about 130 words a minute. About how many words should the speech be?
Of 25 draft replies to questions in Parliament, 20 were sent to the Minister's office on time. What percentage is this?
What term is used for brief points, rather than a full text, given to a Minister to guide what to say at a meeting?
What word describes the security grading given to a document, such as "confidential" or "secret"?

essays.stem: You are asked to prepare a Cabinet submission seeking approval for a youth employment programme costing J$600,000,000 over three years. Plan how you would prepare it, from receiving the request to sending it forward.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would confirm with my director exactly what Cabinet is being asked to decide, the deadline and the format required by the Cabinet Office guidelines. I would set up a secure file and a version log, and limit access to those who need it. I would gather evidence: youth unemployment figures, the programme design, results of similar programmes and the costs, which average J$200,000,000 a year. I would then consult the finance ministry on funding, the ministry's legal officers on any legal changes, and agencies such as the training and labour bodies that will help deliver it, recording their views. Next I would draft the submission under the standard headings: purpose, background, discussion with options, consultations, financial implications, legal implications, risks, communication and the decisions sought. I would write in plain, neutral language, check every figure twice and have a colleague proofread it. The draft would go through clearance by my director and the Permanent Secretary, with changes logged. Finally, the approved version would be signed, sent through the secure channel and filed in the official records.
markingPoints: Confirms the decision sought, deadline and required format
Sets up secure handling and version control
Gathers evidence and consults finance, legal and delivery agencies
Drafts under the standard headings in plain, neutral language, checking figures
Obtains clearance, sends securely and files the record

essays.stem: Bus operators in May Pen have threatened to strike over a new route licence fee. Explain how you would structure a one-page briefing note for the Minister before she meets them, and what you would put under each heading.
essays.modelAnswer: Under Purpose, I would state in one sentence that the note prepares the Minister for her meeting with the operators on a given date and seeks her agreement to a negotiating position. Under Issue, I would summarise the problem: operators object to the new fee and have threatened to strike, which would affect thousands of commuters. Under Background, I would give only the key facts: when and why the fee was introduced, how much it is, how many operators are affected and what consultation took place. Under Considerations or Options, I would set out two or three realistic options, such as keeping the fee, phasing it in over two years, or linking it to route improvements, each with its cost, benefits and risks, including the likely public and media reaction. Under Recommendation, I would state clearly which option is advised and why. I would add short speaking notes and likely questions with suggested answers. The note would carry the date, file reference, author and clearance, and a security marking if needed.
markingPoints: States the purpose and the issue briefly at the start
Gives only the relevant background facts
Sets out realistic options with costs, benefits and risks
Gives a clear, reasoned recommendation
Adds speaking notes or likely questions and the document details

essays.stem: Explain how you would keep a sensitive document secure while drafting, storing and sending it, and what you would do if it were leaked.
essays.modelAnswer: While drafting, I would mark the document with its security classification on every page and work only on official, password-protected equipment, never on a personal computer or account. I would share drafts only with people who need them, using version numbers and a log of who received each version. For storage, electronic copies would sit in a restricted folder with access limited by name, and paper copies would be locked away when not in use, following a clear-desk rule. Unwanted copies would be shredded, not thrown away. For sending, I would use the approved secure government system or, for paper, a sealed, marked envelope delivered by hand or trusted courier, and confirm receipt. I would not discuss the content in public places or on unsecured phones. If a leak happened, I would report it at once to my manager and the security or information officer, as policy requires, and record what was leaked, when and to whom. I would help find how it happened, and the ministry would decide on steps such as warning those affected and preparing lines for the media, then fix the weakness.
markingPoints: Marks the classification and uses only official, secure equipment
Shares on a need-to-know basis with version control and a distribution log
Stores securely (restricted folders, locked storage, shredding)
Sends by approved secure channels and confirms receipt
Reports a leak at once, records details and helps fix the cause

essays.stem: Describe how you would prepare a draft answer for the Minister to a question in Parliament about the number of social housing units completed in the last two years.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first read the exact wording of the question carefully, note the deadline and check whether the same issue has been answered before, using Hansard and the ministry's files. I would then collect the figures from the housing agency's records, for each year and, if useful, by parish, and confirm them with the officer responsible, keeping a note of the source. The draft answer would be short, accurate and factual, answering exactly what was asked in plain language, without political comment. For example, it would give the number of units completed each year and the total. I would then prepare background notes for the Minister: how the figures compare with targets, reasons for any shortfall, units under construction, costs, and likely supplementary questions with suggested answers. I would make sure the figures match what the ministry has published before, or explain any difference. The draft would go through clearance by my director and the Permanent Secretary before reaching the Minister's office in good time. Finally, I would file the final answer and notes for future reference.
markingPoints: Reads the question carefully, notes the deadline and checks past answers
Collects and confirms accurate figures from reliable sources
Writes a short, factual, neutral answer to exactly what was asked
Prepares background notes and supplementary questions with answers
Obtains clearance in time and files the material

essays.stem: Compare how you would write a speech for a Minister, a briefing note for a Minister and a letter for the Permanent Secretary's signature, in terms of purpose, structure and tone.
essays.modelAnswer: A speech is written to be heard by an audience, such as at a school opening or a conference. Its purpose is to inform and inspire, and it reflects the Minister's voice. It needs a strong opening, a few clear messages, short sentences, examples and a memorable close, and figures should be few and rounded. The tone is warm and confident but must remain accurate and non-partisan when written by a public officer. A briefing note is written for one busy reader who must understand an issue or make a decision. Its structure is tight: purpose, issue, background, options and a recommendation, usually on one or two pages. The tone is neutral, analytical and frank, giving impartial advice even when it is unwelcome. A letter for the Permanent Secretary's signature speaks for the ministry to an individual or organisation. It follows a formal layout with reference, date, salutation and the signatory's title, and it answers the reader's points clearly. The tone is courteous and respectful, and plain enough for the reader to understand. All three must be accurate, checked and cleared before use.
markingPoints: Describes the speech: purpose, structure for listening, tone
Describes the briefing note: purpose, tight structure, neutral analytical tone
Describes the letter: purpose, formal layout, courteous tone
Makes clear comparisons between the three
Notes that all must be accurate and cleared

essays.stem: A senior official asks you to change the figures in a report to the Cabinet so that a programme looks more successful than it is. Explain your duties and how you would respond.
essays.modelAnswer: As a public officer, my duty is to give honest, accurate and impartial advice, so that Ministers and Cabinet make decisions on true information. Changing figures to mislead would break the code of conduct and the public service's core values of integrity and honesty, and it could lead to poor decisions and wasted public money. It would also damage trust if discovered, including through an access to information request or an audit. I would respond calmly and professionally. First, I would check that I understand the request, as the official may be asking me to present the true figures more clearly rather than to change them. If the request really is to change facts, I would explain politely that I cannot alter the figures, and offer alternatives: for example, presenting the results fairly with the reasons for any shortfall and the actions planned, or adding context such as progress made. I would keep a note of the conversation. If the pressure continued, I would raise the matter with a more senior officer or through the ministry's proper channels for such concerns.
markingPoints: States the duty of honest, accurate, impartial advice
Explains why changing figures is wrong and its consequences
Clarifies the request and responds calmly
Offers a legitimate alternative presentation of the results
Records the conversation and escalates through proper channels if needed

essays.stem: A colleague's draft briefing note is three pages of background, with the recommendation in the last line, several unexplained abbreviations and no options. Evaluate the draft and explain how you would help improve it.
essays.modelAnswer: The draft does not meet the needs of a busy Minister. Three pages of background bury the issue, so the reader may not see quickly what is being asked or why it matters. Placing the recommendation in the last line, with no summary at the start, makes the note slow to use. With no options, the Minister cannot see what alternatives were considered, their costs and risks, so the advice does not look impartial or complete. Unexplained abbreviations make the note harder to read and may cause errors. I would give feedback privately and constructively, starting with what is good, such as accurate research. I would suggest restructuring under clear headings: purpose and a short summary of the issue and action sought at the top, only the background the reader needs, two or three options with pros, cons and costs, then a clear recommendation linked to the analysis. Detailed background could go in an annex. I would suggest spelling out each abbreviation on first use and keeping the note to one or two pages. I would offer to review the revised version before clearance.
markingPoints: Identifies that excessive background buries the issue
Identifies the problem of the late recommendation and missing summary
Identifies the missing options and their effect on impartial advice
Identifies the abbreviation problem
Gives constructive feedback with a clear restructuring plan

essays.stem: A member of the public has complained to the Minister that her late husband's pension has not been paid for six months. Investigation shows the ministry made an error. Explain how you would write the reply for the Minister's signature.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first gather the facts: the dates, the cause of the error, the amount owed and when it will be paid, and check them with the pensions unit. The letter would carry a file reference and date, and be addressed correctly to the widow. I would open with sincere condolences on the loss of her husband, then thank her for writing. I would admit plainly that the ministry made an error and apologise, without hiding behind jargon or blaming individual staff. I would explain briefly what went wrong, in plain language, and state exactly what is being done: for example, the full amount owed, stated in J$, to be paid by a set date, and regular payments from the next month. I would give her a named contact officer and phone number for questions. I would mention what the ministry has changed to prevent the same error. The tone would be warm, respectful and clear throughout. The draft would protect her personal data, be checked for accuracy, and be cleared by senior officers before it reaches the Minister.
markingPoints: Checks the facts and the amounts with the responsible unit
Opens with sincere condolences and thanks
Admits the error and apologises clearly, without blaming staff
States the remedy with amounts, dates and a named contact
Uses a warm, respectful, plain tone, protects data and obtains clearance

essays.stem: On Monday you are told that a sensitive policy paper must reach the Permanent Secretary by Thursday at noon. Four units must be consulted. Explain how you would plan and manage the work to meet the deadline.
essays.modelAnswer: On Monday morning I would confirm the scope, the decision sought, the format and the length with my director, and agree who must clear the paper. I would then work backwards from Thursday noon: final clearance by the director on Wednesday afternoon, consultation comments back by Wednesday morning, a first draft by Monday evening. I would contact the four units at once, explain the deadline, send them the specific questions I need answered and name a contact in each unit. By Monday evening I would circulate a draft securely, marked with its version number and classification, asking for comments by 10:00 a.m. Wednesday. I would block my own time to research and write, putting routine work aside after agreeing this with my manager. On Tuesday I would follow up any unit that has not replied and warn my director early of any risk. On Wednesday I would merge the comments, record how each was dealt with, check facts and figures twice and ask a colleague to proofread. After clearance, I would send the paper securely on Thursday morning and file the final version.
markingPoints: Confirms scope, format and clearance path at the start
Plans backwards from the deadline with interim dates
Engages the four units early with specific questions and deadlines
Manages own time, follows up and warns the director of risks
Merges comments, checks quality, obtains clearance and sends securely

essays.stem: You are writing a report to the board of a public body on complaints from clients, including some about named staff. Explain how the data protection law and the access to information law, by their general purposes, should shape the report.
essays.modelAnswer: The general purpose of the data protection law is to make sure personal information is collected and used fairly, only for a clear purpose, kept accurate and secure, and not shared more than needed. For this report, I would include only the personal information the board needs to make decisions. In most cases the board needs patterns, numbers and themes, not clients' names, addresses or health details, so I would summarise or anonymise them. Complaints about named staff should be described in a neutral, factual way, and names should be left out unless the board must act on a specific case, in which case those details could go in a confidential annex with limited circulation. The report would be stored and sent securely. The general purpose of the access to information law is to let the public request official documents, subject to exemptions such as personal privacy. I would therefore write the report on the assumption that it may be requested, keeping it accurate, professional and free of opinion or gossip. Keeping personal details separate makes it easier to release the main report, with any protected parts redacted.
markingPoints: States the general purpose of the data protection law correctly
Includes only necessary personal data, summarising or anonymising
Handles complaints about staff neutrally, with details in a restricted annex if needed
States the general purpose of the access to information law and its privacy limits
Writes as if it may be released, keeping personal data separable for redaction

practical1.title: Prepare a ministerial briefing note with speaking notes
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up case pack: a ministry must brief its Minister before a meeting with a group affected by a new policy (for example vendors objecting to a market relocation). The pack holds facts, figures in J$, letters from the group, a legal opinion and press cuttings. Some papers are marked confidential. As a group, prepare a one-page briefing note, speaking notes and likely questions, and take them through clearance. Each member has a named role: researcher and fact-checker (pulls the key facts from the pack and checks every figure twice against the source); drafter (writes the briefing note under the headings purpose, issue, background, options, recommendation); options analyst (prepares a table of two or three options with costs, benefits and risks, including likely public reaction); speaking notes writer (writes the speaking notes and at least six likely questions with suggested answers); and clearance officer (keeps the version log, marks each draft with its version number and classification, reviews the final draft for plain language and accuracy, and signs the clearance sheet). In a group of four, the drafter also writes the speaking notes. Each version must be saved or printed so the assessor can see how the note improved.
materials: Case pack from the assessor, with papers marked confidential
Templates for the briefing note, version log and clearance sheet
Printer, paper and a lockable folder or tray
photos: The researcher's fact sheet with sources marked
The options table with costs, benefits and risks
The first draft and the final briefing note side by side, with version numbers
The speaking notes and likely questions
The version log and signed clearance sheet
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Facts and J$ figures in the note match the sources and were checked twice
The note fits one page and uses the correct headings in plain language
Options are realistic and the recommendation follows from the analysis
Speaking notes and answers are accurate, neutral and suited to the meeting
Each draft carries a version number and classification, and the log is complete
Confidential papers were kept in the folder and returned at the end
safety: Treat the papers marked confidential as you would at work: keep them in the folder and return every copy
Do not photograph confidential pages except the parts the assessor names
Keep comments on each other's drafts respectful and constructive
Take a short screen break each hour

practical2.title: Draft a Cabinet submission and hold a clearance meeting
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up proposal from a public body (for example a ministry seeking approval for a new grant scheme), with costs over three years in J$, consultation responses from other agencies and a request under the access to information law for a related report. Part A (1 hour 15 minutes): draft a short Cabinet submission (two to three pages) under the headings purpose, background, discussion and options, consultations, financial implications, legal implications, risks, communication and decisions sought. Each member drafts at least one section. Part B (30 minutes): role-play a clearance meeting. One member is the director who chairs; one is the legal officer; one is the finance officer; the drafters present and answer questions; one member records the changes asked for in a comments log. Part C (45 minutes): revise the submission from the comments log, and prepare a redacted copy of the related report that removes personal information, ready for release in answer to the request. In a group of four, the director also keeps the comments log.
materials: Case pack and consultation responses from the assessor
Computers with word processing and spreadsheet software
Templates for the submission and comments log
A printed copy of the related report and black markers or a redaction tool
photos: The first draft of the submission with each section's author named
The financial implications table on screen, with totals for each year
The clearance meeting in progress (faces only if all agree)
The comments log showing each change and how it was dealt with
The revised submission and the redacted report
checklist: Drafted a clear, accurate section in neutral, plain language
Financial figures add up correctly across the years and were checked twice
Consultation responses are reported fairly, including any objections
Clearance comments were recorded and acted on
Redaction removes personal information but leaves the rest of the report readable
safety: Keep the case pack and drafts confidential and return all copies to the assessor
Redact carefully: check that no personal details remain visible or readable on screen
Keep the clearance meeting respectful; comment on the text, not the writer
Photograph faces only if every person agrees and the Centre allows it
